paragraphs.heading: A network in California
paragraphs.text: The Wood–Anderson seismograph, developed by Anderson, was among the first practical instruments that could record seismic waves. Wood then built a network of seismographs that stretched across Southern California. He also recruited Charles Richter, then young and unknown. The job was to measure the seismograms and to locate the earthquakes that produced the seismic waves.

paragraphs.heading: Curves from Japan
paragraphs.text: In 1931 Kiyoo Wadati showed how, for several strong earthquakes in Japan, he had measured the amplitude of the shaking at various distances from the epicenter. He then plotted distance against the logarithm of the amplitude. The curves he found correlated roughly with the estimated magnitudes of the earthquakes. Richter resolved some difficulties with this method. Working with data that his colleague Beno Gutenberg had collected, he then produced curves of the same kind. This confirmed that such curves could be used to compare the relative magnitudes of one earthquake and another.

paragraphs.heading: Three choices
paragraphs.text: More work was needed to turn this into a practical way of assigning an absolute measure of magnitude. First, the possible values cover a wide range, and to span it Richter took up a suggestion from Gutenberg and used a logarithmic scale. Astronomers use a similar magnitude scale for the brightness of stars. Second, he wanted magnitude zero to sit around the limit of what people can perceive. Third, he named one standard instrument for producing seismograms, the Wood–Anderson seismograph.

paragraphs.heading: The definition
paragraphs.text: With those choices made, magnitude was defined as the logarithm of the largest trace amplitude, given in microns and measured 100 km away. The scale was calibrated with a magnitude 0 shock. That is a shock which, at 100 km, shows a largest amplitude of 1 μm, or 0.001 mm, on a seismogram from a Wood-Anderson torsion seismometer. As a last step, Richter worked out a table of corrections for distance.

paragraphs.heading: What the numbers mean
paragraphs.text: The common logarithms are there simply to keep the measurements manageable. Going from magnitude 3 to magnitude 5 means the measured amplitude of the seismic waves is a hundred times greater. In terms of energy, each increase of 0.2 corresponds to roughly a doubling of the energy released. An event above magnitude 4.5 is strong enough for a seismograph anywhere in the world to record it, as long as its sensors are not in the shadow of the earthquake.

paragraphs.heading: Where the scale breaks down
paragraphs.text: The scale was defined in 1935 with particular circumstances and particular instruments in mind. The circumstances were those of Southern California. The instrument would become saturated by strong earthquakes and could not record high values. The moment magnitude scale was introduced in 1979 and gradually became the preferred way to measure large earthquakes. The local magnitude scale is still used for smaller earthquakes that are nearby. Above magnitude 8, the Richter scale becomes meaningless.

paragraphs.heading: How big earthquakes get
paragraphs.text: Millions of minor earthquakes happen around the world every year. Earthquakes of magnitude 8.0 or more happen about once a year, on average. The largest one recorded is the Great Chilean earthquake, which struck on May 22, 1960, and measured 9.5 on the moment magnitude scale. The seismologist Susan Hough has suggested that magnitude 10 may be a very rough upper limit on what the tectonic zones of the Earth can produce.
